title: The Telescope Turned Skyward
places: Syon House on the Thames, west of London
Trefenty, Carmarthenshire, observing with his neighbour John Prothero
intro: In the autumn of 1608 a spectacle-maker from Middelburg brought a tube with two lenses to The Hague, where the Dutch Republic was negotiating a truce with Spain and receiving, that same season, an embassy from the King of Siam. Within three years the same simple device had shown the Moon's mountains, four moons circling Jupiter, Saturn's strange shape, the phases of Venus and spots on the Sun, and Rome's leading astronomers had said in writing that these things were really there. This chapter follows the instrument from patent office to sky, and the race to see, record and claim what it showed. Almost none of the record here is a diary in the ordinary sense. It is government minutes (Lipperhey and Metius), observing notebooks and dated drawings (Harriot, Galileo), letters that functioned as priority claims, including Galileo's ciphered anagrams, printed books with dated dedications (Sidereus Nuncius, Kepler's Dissertatio and Narratio, Marius's Mundus Iovialis), a hostile pamphlet (Horky), and a formal oration (Maelcote). Each eye's form is tagged honestly. Where only a month or a later account survives, the entry says so. The heart of the chapter is who knew what, and when. Thomas Harriot, a mathematician living on the Earl of Northumberland's pension at Syon House, drew the Moon through a Dutch glass in July 1609 by English reckoning, months before Galileo; he published nothing. Galileo, in Padua, improved the tube fastest, saw what it implied, and printed within weeks of his Jupiter discovery. In Protestant Ansbach, Simon Marius watched the same moons and later claimed to have recorded them first, a claim that hinges partly on a ten-day calendar difference and partly on a log he never produced. The claims ledger sets out these positions with their evidence; it does not judge them. Around the observers stand the people who carried the news, doubted it, and confirmed it: Paolo Sarpi in Venice, who read the Hague news-sheet; Giambattista della Porta in Naples, who thought it was his idea and no great thing; Kepler in Prague, who backed Galileo before he could look and then looked; Martin Horky, a student in Bologna who saw Galileo's own demonstration and declared it an illusion; William Lower in Wales, comparing the Moon to a tart; and the Jesuits of the Collegio Romano, Clavius and Maelcote, whose assent in April and May 1611 turned a contested claim into accepted fact. The visible record in these years is almost entirely male and European. Lens-grinders, assistants such as Harriot's helper Christopher Tooke, and the unnamed workmen and pedlars who spread cheap spyglasses from the Netherlands to Paris and Milan by spring 1609 did much of the work but left little writing of their own; where they appear, it is through others' papers.

title: A Black Drop on the Sun: The Transits of Venus
eyes: Guillaume Le Gentil de la Galaisière
places: Portsmouth (letter dated there); the Seahorse forced back to Plymouth
At sea, Indian Ocean, aboard a French frigate
His house on the Moika, St Petersburg
Prince of Wales Fort, Churchill River
San José del Cabo, Baja California
Hill above Real de Santa Ana, Baja California
Prince of Wales Fort, Hudson Bay
Royal Danish Society of Sciences, Copenhagen
At sea in the Indian Ocean
The roof of his own house on the Moika, St Petersburg
intro: On 6 June 1761 and again on 3–4 June 1769, Venus passed across the face of the sun, a pair of events that would not come again until 1874 and 1882. Edmond Halley had shown in 1716 that if observers far apart on the Earth timed the planet's entry and exit, the small differences in their times would give the distance to the sun, the unit by which the whole solar system is measured. To do it, astronomers had to be at the ends of the Earth at the same hour, with good clocks, known positions and clear skies. What followed was the first planned world-wide scientific collaboration. In 1761, despite the Seven Years' War, about 120 observers at some 60 sites took part; in 1769, about 150 observations came from 77 stations, from Hudson Bay to Tahiti and from Vardø to Baja California. The convergence days in this chapter are the transit days themselves: on each, eight or more of these eyes are looking at the same small black disc from places thousands of kilometres apart. The honest record is mostly not private diaries. It is observing logs and published reports, letters dated to establish what was sent when, travel journals written up afterwards (Chappe, Le Gentil), and a few true diaries (Sajnovics at Vardø, Wales's weather journal at Churchill, Cook's ship's journal). The form tags say which is which. Some eyes appear through letters about their work rather than their own words, and the Russian stations are thinly documented here. Laid side by side, the entries show the race in an odd form. It was not a race between rivals for one discovery, but a race against weather, war, epidemic and the post. Chappe saw both transits and died of the second; Le Gentil waited eight years and saw neither; Mason and Dixon nearly turned back after a sea battle; Hell's late report led to an accusation of fraud that took a century to clear. One observer, Lomonosov, saw something no one asked him to look for and claimed an atmosphere around Venus, a claim still argued over. The claims ledger follows the numbers. The 1761 results gave values for the solar parallax (the angle that fixes the sun's distance) ranging from about 8.3 to over 10 seconds of arc. The 1769 reductions published between 1770 and 1774, by William Smith, Hornsby, Lalande, Pingré, Lexell, Planman and Hell, narrowed it to 8.43–8.80 seconds. Encke's re-reduction of 1824 gave 8.58 seconds, and the modern value is about 8.794. The ledger reports these as each computer's claims, not as a verdict.

title: The Body on the Execution Ground: Anatomy, Translation and Credit in Edo
eyes: Dejima Dagregisters: opperhoofden Daniel Armenault and Arend Willem Feith
places: Ani copper mine and Kakunodate, Akita
Edo: Kotsugahara, the translation table, the Nagasakiya inn where the Dutch lodged
Edo, the translation table and the Nagasakiya
Kyoto, the dissection of an executed man
intro: Before dawn on the fourth day of the third month of Meiwa 8 (18 April 1771 in the Western calendar), three physicians walked out to Kotsugahara, the execution ground at Senju on Edo's northern edge. Sugita Genpaku and Nakagawa Jun'an were doctors to the Obama domain. Maeno Ryōtaku served the Nakatsu domain and was nearly fifty. Each of them carried a Dutch anatomy book that none of them could read: Ontleedkundige Tafelen, the 1734 Amsterdam translation of Johann Adam Kulmus's Anatomische Tabellen (Danzig, 1722). The body was that of a woman of about fifty, born in Kyoto and executed for a serious crime. Edo people knew her only by a nickname, Aochababa, the 'green-tea hag'. Her name is not recorded. The man who did the cutting is the most important person in the story who left no writing of his own. Dissection was work for the outcaste community (eta and hinin), the same people whose hereditary trades included handling dead cattle and horses. The usual dissector, Toramatsu, was ill that day. His grandfather, about ninety and still strong, took his place. As Sugita remembered it, the old man had opened bodies since his youth and named each organ as he went. He pointed out structures he had no name for and said they were always in the same place. He also remarked that the physicians who had watched before him never asked him anything. The Dutch plates matched what he showed them. The Chinese charts of the 'five viscera and six bowels' did not. This chapter does not describe the body. It follows the record: who looked, what they compared, and what they did next. On the walk home the three men agreed to translate the book themselves, without relying on the Nagasaki interpreters. They started the next day at Maeno's lodging in the Nakatsu residence at Teppōzu. Maeno knew the most Dutch, after about a hundred days of study in Nagasaki in 1770 and a dictionary he had bought there. Katsuragawa Hoshū, the young son of a shogunal physician, soon joined them. The work went word by word, and it took three years and many drafts. A trial booklet of plates, Kaitai Yakuzu, came out in 1773. The full Kaitai Shinsho was published in 1774. Its plates were drawn by Odano Naotake, an Akita samurai painter whom the polymath Hiraga Gennai had trained in Western-style drawing and introduced to Sugita. The race in this chapter runs against ignorance and caution, not against a rival laboratory. The prologue belongs to Yamawaki Tōyō in Kyoto, who saw a beheaded man dissected in 1754 and published Zōshi in 1759. That was the first Japanese account of an observed dissection, and Sugita knew of it. The question of priority is really a question of credit. Maeno Ryōtaku, who did more of the translating than anyone else, would not let his name go on the book. The title page names Sugita as translator, Nakagawa as collator and Katsuragawa as reviewer. title: Two Notebooks, One Theory
eyes: Linnean Society of London (meeting record and Journal)
places: Moor Park water-cure, Surrey (letter headed Down)
intro: In the early summer of 1858 a packet from the Moluccas reached Down House in Kent. Inside was a twenty-page essay by Alfred Russel Wallace, a collector Darwin had never met, setting out the theory Darwin had kept in notebooks, sketches and an unfinished book for twenty years. What happened in the next fortnight was decided by letters: Darwin to Lyell, Darwin to Hooker, Lyell and Hooker to the Linnean Society. All of it happened while Darwin's baby son was dying of scarlet fever. This chapter is built almost entirely from notebooks and dated letters, not diaries, and the form tags say so. The heart of it is the priority ledger: Darwin's 1838 notebook, his 1842 sketch and 1844 essay, the abstract he sent to Asa Gray in 1857, Wallace's 1855 'Sarawak Law' and his 1858 essay. On 1 July 1858 these were laid side by side and read in date order to a society that recorded no discussion. Several key documents are missing: Wallace's covering letter to Darwin, and Hooker's and Darwin's letters back to him. The gaps are where the arguments are. Darwin dated his letter to Lyell only '18', and Lyell's endorsement supplies June. Wallace's letter to Henry Bates's brother, posted from Ternate in early March, reached London on 3 June. That led some historians (Brooks, Brackman, Davies) to argue that Darwin had the essay for weeks before he admitted it. Van Wyhe and Rookmaaker reconstructed the mail routes and argue it left Ternate a month later and arrived when Darwin said. Others dispute even where Wallace wrote it, Ternate or Dodinga on Gilolo. These are set out as positions; the book takes no side. Around the two principals stand the men who held the evidence: Lyell, who wrote Darwin's theory into his own notebook in 1856 and told him to publish; Hooker, who had read the 1844 essay; and Gray at Harvard, holding the 1857 letter. Emma Darwin's terse pocket diary records the household side: nurses, a sister arriving, children sent away. Far off are Bates on the Amazon, Wallace's oldest friend, and Ali, the young Sarawak Malay who collected much of what Wallace studied and who left no words of his own. He is seen only through Wallace and is flagged as such. The chapter ends with the Origin's publication on 24 November 1859, Huxley's letter of the day before, and Wallace's letters of the day after and a year later. Those letters show Wallace without a trace of resentment. Thomas Bell's verdict that the year had brought no striking discoveries is a reminder that, inside the room, the turn of history was not visible.

title: The Glow in the Shed: The Curies and the Race for the Rays
eyes: Comptes rendus hebdomadaires des séances de l'Académie des sciences
places: Académie des sciences, Paris (presented by Lippmann)
The ESPCI workshop and storeroom, rue Vauquelin, Paris
Muséum national d'histoire naturelle, Jardin des Plantes, Paris
ESPCI and the Sorbonne laboratories, Paris
Institut de France, quai de Conti, Paris
intro: In eleven years, from a darkened room in Würzburg in November 1895 to a rain-slick street on the Left Bank in April 1906, physics found out that atoms are not permanent. The story is usually told as one woman's triumph, and Marie Curie earns that. But the record is a relay and a race. A German professor saw a screen glow across his laboratory. A Paris physicist, nudged by a question at the Académie, wrapped photographic plates in black paper and was rescued by bad weather. A Polish doctoral student chose his rays for her thesis because no one had yet written much about them, and within months she was racing a German she had never met. This chapter is built less from diaries than from the instruments of priority: laboratory notebooks, papers whose dates were fixed by the weekly sittings of the Académie des sciences, manuscripts signed off with a place and a day, and letters that bent a prize. That is said plainly here because it is the honest shape of the record. Röntgen had most of his personal papers burned on his own instruction. Becquerel is known through short notes in the Comptes rendus. The Curies' own laboratory notebooks survive at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, so contaminated by the radium they handled that readers sign a waiver and the most affected sheets are encapsulated. Lay the dates side by side and the race becomes visible. Gerhard Schmidt told the German Physical Society on 24 March 1898 that thorium gives off Becquerel rays; Marie Curie's note saying the same, and more, was presented in Paris nineteen days later. In Cambridge, Ernest Rutherford dated his manuscript naming alpha and beta rays on 1 September 1898; in Paris the Curies were already writing 'radio-active' into the title of their polonium note. In Montreal on 13 September 1899 Rutherford signed off a paper describing a radiation that fell to half its strength in about a minute — the first clear measurement of what would be called a half-life — while across the Atlantic André Debierne was drawing yet another new substance out of the Curies' pitchblende residues. Then the human seam. When the French Academy's eminent members put forward Becquerel and Pierre Curie for the 1903 Nobel Prize, Marie's name was not on their letters. A Swedish mathematician, Gösta Mittag-Leffler, warned Pierre; Pierre wrote back that he wished to be considered together with her. The Nobel archive shows another 1903 nomination, by Charles Bouchard, that named all three, and lists two 1902 nominations, by Gaston Darboux and Emil Warburg, that already included her; the Association Curie et Joliot-Curie dates Bouchard's nomination of her to 1902 instead. The book reports these documents as positions in the record, not as a verdict. The chapter ends with the accident of 19 April 1906 and the private journal Marie kept for a year afterwards, addressed to Pierre. Extracts from that journal first appeared in print in 1937 and a full French edition only in 2022; it is digested here, never quote

title: The Christmas Walk: Splitting the Nucleus
places: Old Grove Road, Nassau Point, Peconic
Institut du Radium, rue Pierre-Curie, Paris
Laboratoire de chimie nucléaire, Collège de France, Paris
Old Grove Road, Nassau Point, Peconic, Long Island
intro: For four years after 1934 the best laboratories in Europe bombarded uranium with neutrons and read the results the wrong way. Enrico Fermi's group in Rome believed they had made elements heavier than uranium; Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin spent years mapping a growing family of supposed 'transuranes'; Irène Joliot-Curie in Paris found a substance that behaved stubbornly like lanthanum and could not explain it. A chemist, Ida Noddack, had suggested in print as early as 1934 that the nucleus might simply break into large pieces. Almost nobody took her up on it. The answer arrived in the middle of a political catastrophe. Meitner, Austrian-born and of Jewish descent, lost the protection of her passport when Germany annexed Austria and slipped across the Dutch border on 13 July 1938. Five months later Hahn and Strassmann, still in Berlin, found barium — an element roughly half the weight of uranium — among their products. Hahn wrote to Meitner in Stockholm before he wrote to anyone else. Over Christmas, in the small Swedish town of Kungälv, Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out on a walk in the snow that the uranium nucleus, pictured as a wobbling liquid drop, had split in two and released an enormous quantity of energy. This chapter is built almost entirely from dated letters, laboratory notebooks and the received and published dates of scientific papers rather than from diaries. That is where the record of this discovery lives: Hahn and Meitner wrote to each other every few days, and those letters — together with Hahn's and Meitner's pocket diaries and the notebook pages from Berlin and Copenhagen — establish who knew what, and when. Two of the eyes (Laura Fermi, Leó Szilárd) are known chiefly through later memoirs and recollections, and they are tagged that way. Because all of this material is modern and in copyright, the entries are paraphrased digests and carry no quotations. Put the eyes side by side and a race appears that none of them fully saw at the time. Frisch told Niels Bohr in Copenhagen on 3 January 1939; Bohr carried the secret across the Atlantic and, though he meant to protect Meitner and Frisch's priority, the news slipped out at Princeton the day he landed. Within days of his announcement in Washington on 26 January, laboratories in New York, Washington, Baltimore, Berkeley and Paris had reproduced the effect. By March the Paris team of Frédéric Joliot, Hans von Halban and Lew Kowarski, and two groups at Columbia, had shown that each split released extra neutrons — the condition for a chain reaction. Szilárd, who had been afraid of exactly this since 1933, tried and failed to persuade physicists to stop publishing, and by August had Albert Einstein's signature on a letter to President Roosevelt. The coda is the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, given in November 1945 to Hahn alone. Historians have argued over that decision ever since; the chapter reports their positions and the evidence they cite, not

title: Two Chains, Many Hands: The Double Helix
places: Basement X-ray room, King's College London
Cambridge, on the way to Brussels
Basement X-ray laboratory beneath the Strand, London
The Cavendish Laboratory, Free School Lane, and his home in Portugal Place, Cambridge
Cambridge, with trips to King's College London
The Cavendish office shared with Watson and Crick
intro: In the winter of 1952–53 the structure of DNA was worked on in three places at once. At King's College London, in a basement under the Strand, Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Raymond Gosling were taking X-ray photographs of DNA fibres and analysing them by slow, careful mathematics. Down the corridor, and on bad terms with her, Maurice Wilkins was working on the same molecule. Fifty miles away at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Francis Crick and James Watson had been told to leave DNA to King's, and were building models anyway. In Pasadena, Linus Pauling, the most famous chemist in the world, had sent off a structure of his own. This chapter is built mostly from notebooks, letters, typescripts and the published papers, not diaries. Franklin's laboratory notebooks and her dated draft of March 1953 survive at the Churchill Archives Centre in Cambridge, and many are online through the US National Library of Medicine. The Pauling family's letters and Linus Pauling's research notes are digitised by Oregon State University. Letters between Wilkins and Crick are at Cold Spring Harbor and King's College London. Several of the best-known scenes, though, come from accounts written much later. Watson's The Double Helix (1968) is a memoir published fifteen years on, and its portrait of Franklin has been disputed ever since. Other later sources include Gosling's interviews, Wilkins's 2003 autobiography, Perutz's 1969 letter defending himself, and Aaron Klug's analyses of Franklin's notebooks. Each of these is marked as later testimony where it is used. The heart of the chapter is a question of timing: who knew what, and when. Two documents have carried most of the argument. One is Photograph 51, the B-form pattern taken in May 1952, which Wilkins showed Watson on 30 January 1953. The other is the December 1952 report of the King's unit to a Medical Research Council committee, which Max Perutz passed to the Cambridge pair in February 1953. Some writers have called this a theft of Franklin's data. Others, including Gosling in later life, Perutz, and the historians Matthew Cobb and Nathaniel Comfort, describe something more tangled: informal sharing within a small British community, with Franklin as an equal member of a scattered four-person effort. On this view her credit was understated rather than stolen. The book records each position and the evidence offered for it, and gives no verdict of its own. What the notebooks do settle is that Franklin was moving under her own power. Between 19 January and 24 February 1953 her notes take her from a two-chain antiparallel A form to the conclusion that both forms are two-chain helices with the phosphates on the outside. Her draft paper is dated 17 March 1953, one day before the Watson–Crick manuscript reached King's. Klug, who knew her work best, judged that she was still a step or two short of base-pairing.
